fuentes/carta-abierta-a-los-aficionados/.texto: Letter dated 3 February 1976, published in the Homebrew Computer Club newsletter, in which Bill Gates, then a partner in a small Micro-Soft, complains that most hobbyists use copies of Altair BASIC without paying for it. He estimates that the work put into it was worth more than $40,000 and asks who will write good software if no one pays for it. Many hobbyists replied that the program was expensive and that sharing was the custom of the community.

It is the first public statement that software is a product sold under license, seven years before the GNU project and nine before the GNU Manifesto: it was not a response to Stallman but a precursor of the model he would challenge.

fuentes/anuncio-gnu/resumen.texto: Message of 27 September 1983 in the newsgroups net.unix-wizards and net.usoft in which Stallman announces that he will write a complete Unix-compatible operating system, called GNU (“GNU's Not Unix”), and give it away to anyone who wants to use it. He asks manufacturers for donations of machines and programmers for time and code.

fuentes/anuncio-gnu/por_que_importa.texto: It is the founding charter of the free software movement, written as the shared code of MIT was giving way to commercial licenses.

fuentes/manifiesto-gnu/resumen.texto: Published in March 1985 in Dr. Dobb's magazine, it explains why Stallman is writing GNU: the “Golden Rule” of sharing a program one likes, as opposed to licenses that divide users. It answers objections (how programmers will get paid, who will provide support) and proposes making a living from services, customization and donations.

fuentes/manifiesto-gnu/por_que_importa.texto: It is the founding text of free software. It does not answer Gates's 1976 letter (it does not mention it), but it disputes the model of software sold under license that the letter defended.

fuentes/definicion-de-software-libre/sop.texto: GNU's Bulletin, later a page on gnu.org

fuentes/definicion-de-software-libre/res.texto: First published in the February 1986 GNU's Bulletin, it defines free software in terms of freedom rather than price (“free as in free speech, not as in free beer”). In its current form it lists four freedoms: to run the program for any purpose, to study and modify it (with access to the source code), to redistribute copies, and to distribute modified versions.

fuentes/definicion-de-software-libre/por.texto: It is the standard by which the FSF judges licenses and programs, and the basis of the Open Source Definition.

fuentes/gpl/resumen.texto: Copyright license that allows a program to be used, studied, copied and modified on condition that distributed versions keep the same license and the source code (“copyleft”). Version 1 dates from 1989, version 2 from 1991 (the one used by the Linux kernel), and version 3, from 2007, drafted with Eben Moglen after a public debate, adds provisions against patents and against devices that prevent the installation of modified versions.

fuentes/gpl/por_que_importa.texto: It used copyright to guarantee the freedom to copy. Its critics, from Microsoft to supporters of permissive licenses such as BSD, object that this condition “infects” the programs that incorporate it.

fuentes/el-derecho-a-leer/soporte.texto: Short story in Communications of the ACM

fuentes/el-derecho-a-leer/resumen.texto: Short story published in February 1997 set in a future in which lending an e-book or one's own computer is a crime, and debuggers require a license. A student, Lissa, asks her classmate Dan to lend her his computer, and he must choose between helping her and obeying the law.

fuentes/el-derecho-a-leer/por_que_import.texto: It anticipated the debates over digital rights management and the 1998 DMCA; Stallman added notes tracking the laws that brought that fiction closer to reality.

fuentes/software-libre-para-una-sociedad.texto: Collection of essays by Stallman edited by Joshua Gay: the GNU Manifesto, the Free Software Definition, “Why Software Should Not Have Owners”, “The Right to Read”, and texts on patents and copyleft. It insists that the issue is ethical rather than technical and on distinguishing free software from open source.
It is the most complete exposition of the philosophy of free software; the Spanish edition by Traficantes de Sueños (2004) circulates under a free license.
Spanish edition by Traficantes de Sueños, under a free license

fuentes/anuncio-de-linux/resumen.texto: Message of 25 August 1991 in which a student in Helsinki says he is making a free operating system for 386 computers, “just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu”. He asks MINIX users for their opinions on which features they want.

fuentes/anuncio-de-linux/por_que_importa.texto: It is the beginning of the Linux kernel, which, combined with the GNU tools, produced a complete free operating system, the basis of a large share of today's servers and phones.

fuentes/anuncio-de-linux/leer.0.titulo.texto: Original message in the Usenet archive

fuentes/linux-es-obsoleto/resumen.texto: Message of 29 January 1992 in which Tanenbaum criticizes Linux for being a monolithic kernel rather than a microkernel and for depending on the 386 architecture; Torvalds replies defending his practical design. The exchange, with other participants, is known as the Tanenbaum–Torvalds debate.

fuentes/linux-es-obsoleto/por_que_import.texto: It shows a technical discussion held in public and within an open community, the way of working that Raymond would later call the “bazaar”.

fuentes/linux-es-obsoleto/leer.0.titulo.texto: The full debate, appendix to the book Open Sources (O'Reilly)

fuentes/manifiesto-debian/resumen.texto: Text of January 1994 in which Ian Murdock explains that Debian will be a GNU/Linux distribution made “openly”, in the spirit of Linux and GNU, by volunteers rather than by a for-profit company. The Free Software Foundation sponsored the project from 1994 to 1995.

fuentes/manifiesto-debian/por_que_import.texto: It set the model of a community distribution, which Debian still follows and from which Ubuntu and many others derive, among them the Argentine Huayra.

fuentes/contrato-social-de-debian/resume.texto: Commitment of the Debian project, approved in July 1997: Debian will always remain free software, will give its improvements back to the community, will not hide problems and will be guided by the needs of its users. It includes the Debian Free Software Guidelines (DFSG), the criteria for accepting a license.

fuentes/contrato-social-de-debian/por_qu.texto: The DFSG, written by Bruce Perens, became the 1998 Open Source Definition almost unchanged.

fuentes/la-catedral-y-el-bazar/resumen.texto: Essay presented in May 1997 at the Linux Kongress in Würzburg that compares two ways of making software: the “cathedral”, with closed releases planned by a few, and the “bazaar” of Linux, with early and frequent releases open to all. It formulates “Linus's law”: “given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow”.

fuentes/la-catedral-y-el-bazar/por_que_i.texto: It defended opening source code for its technical effectiveness rather than on ethical grounds; it influenced Netscape's decision to release its browser and the birth of “open source”.

fuentes/la-catedral-y-el-bazar/leer.1.ti.texto: Spanish translation by José Soto Pino

fuentes/definicion-de-open-source/resume.texto: Ten criteria a license must meet to be open source, adapted by Perens from the Debian guidelines: free redistribution, access to the source code, permission for derived works, no discrimination against persons or uses, among others. The Open Source Initiative applies it to approve licenses.

fuentes/definicion-de-open-source/por_qu.texto: Almost all licenses that meet this definition are also free according to the FSF; the difference between the two movements lies more in the arguments (effectiveness or ethics) than in the licenses.

fuentes/definicion-de-open-source/leer.0.texto: Text on the Open Source Initiative website

fuentes/documentos-halloween/resumen.texto: Internal Microsoft memoranda from 1998 that analyze open-source software, Linux in particular, as a threat to the company and propose, among other strategies, extending standard protocols with proprietary additions to shut it out. Eric Raymond received them as leaks and published them with commentary in November 1998; Microsoft confirmed their authenticity, clarifying that they were technical analyses and not the official position.

fuentes/documentos-halloween/por_que_imp.texto: They showed that Microsoft took the competition from free software seriously, and their authors acknowledged in them the quality of that model.

fuentes/documentos-halloween/leer.0.titu.texto: Halloween Documents with comments by Eric S. Raymond

fuentes/linux-es-un-cancer/resumen.texto: Interview of 1 June 2001 in which Microsoft's chief executive says that Linux “is a cancer that attaches itself in an intellectual property sense to everything it touches”, referring to the GPL's requirement to release derived works. He argues that this is incompatible with the commercial software business.

fuentes/linux-es-un-cancer/por_que_impor.texto: It sums up Microsoft's position on free software at the turn of the century, which the company abandoned in the following decade.

fuentes/linux-es-un-cancer/leer.0.titulo.texto: The Register article on the interview

fuentes/discurso-del-codigo-compartido/s.texto: Speech at New York University's Stern School of Business

fuentes/discurso-del-codigo-compartido/r.texto: Speech of 3 May 2001 in which Mundie argues that the GPL threatens intellectual property and the software industry, and presents “shared source” as an alternative: showing Microsoft's code to certain customers and partners without allowing them to redistribute it. Stallman, Torvalds and others responded publicly.

fuentes/discurso-del-codigo-compartido/p.texto: It is the most articulate statement of the defense of proprietary software against free software at the turn of the century.

fuentes/discurso-del-codigo-compartido/l.texto: Text of the speech on Microsoft's website (Internet Archive)

fuentes/fallo-microsoft-apelacion/titulo.texto: Court of Appeals ruling in United States v. Microsoft

fuentes/fallo-microsoft-apelacion/autor.texto: United States Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit

fuentes/fallo-microsoft-apelacion/resume.texto: Unanimous en banc ruling of 28 June 2001 confirming that Microsoft illegally maintained its monopoly in PC operating systems, but reversing the finding of attempted monopolization of browsers, ordering a reexamination of the finding on tying the browser to Windows and vacating the order to break up the company. It removed Judge Jackson for having given interviews during the proceedings and remanded the case to set a different remedy.

fuentes/fallo-microsoft-apelacion/por_qu.texto: It led to the November 2001 settlement, which required Microsoft to share interfaces with other companies without breaking it up; for some it was a weak sanction, for others an excessive intervention in the market.

fuentes/fallo-microsoft-apelacion/leer.0.texto: Case documents at the Department of Justice

fuentes/dmca/resumen.texto: Law signed by Bill Clinton on 28 October 1998 implementing the 1996 WIPO treaties: it prohibits circumventing technical protection measures on works (digital rights management) and manufacturing tools to do so, and exempts internet providers from liability if they remove content upon notice.

fuentes/dmca/por_que_importa.texto: The cultural industry defends it as protection against mass copying; the EFF and free software advocates criticize it for hindering security research, fair use and interoperability, as in the case of the DeCSS program.

fuentes/dmca/leer.1.titulo.texto: Summary by the United States Copyright Office

fuentes/sopa/autor.texto: Lamar Smith and others (House of Representatives)

fuentes/sopa/resumen.texto: Bill introduced in October 2011 that would have allowed courts to order providers, search engines, payment processors and advertisers to cut off access to foreign sites accused of piracy. Its Senate counterpart was PIPA (PROTECT IP Act), from May 2011.

fuentes/sopa/por_que_importa.texto: Supported by the film and music industries and the Chamber of Commerce, it was withdrawn after the protest blackout of 18 January 2012, which presented it as internet censorship.

fuentes/el-codigo-lessig/titulo.texto: Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace

fuentes/el-codigo-lessig/resumen.texto: Argues that in cyberspace code, that is, the architecture of software, regulates behavior as much as law, the market and social norms (“code is law”). It warns that commerce and governments can program the internet to control it and that those decisions must be debated politically.

fuentes/el-codigo-lessig/por_que_importa.texto: It challenged the idea, spread by Barlow, that the internet was by nature impossible to regulate. Lessig published a second version in 2006, written partly collaboratively and under a free license.

fuentes/el-codigo-lessig/leer.0.titulo.texto: Second version (2006), under a free license

fuentes/cultura-libre-lessig/resumen.texto: Lessig argues that the extension of copyright terms and their application to every digital copy turn a “free culture”, which was always based on taking and transforming what came before, into a “permission culture”. He reviews the history of Disney, radio, film and the Eldred case, and proposes licenses such as those of Creative Commons.

fuentes/cultura-libre-lessig/por_que_imp.texto: It was published under a Creative Commons license on the same day as the print edition and gave its name to the free culture movement; its critics argue that strong copyright is what funds creation.

fuentes/cultura-libre-lessig/leer.0.titu.texto: Book website, under a Creative Commons license

fuentes/licencias-creative-commons/resum.texto: Set of licenses published in December 2002 that allow authors to keep their rights and authorize certain uses in advance (“some rights reserved”), combining conditions: attribution, no derivatives, non-commercial and share-alike. They were adapted to the laws of dozens of countries, including Argentina.

fuentes/licencias-creative-commons/por_q.texto: They are the licenses of Wikipedia (attribution and share-alike), of many open-access journals and of millions of works.

fuentes/fallo-eldred-contra-ashcroft/aut.texto: Supreme Court of the United States

fuentes/fallo-eldred-contra-ashcroft/res.texto: Ruling of 15 January 2003 that, by seven votes to two, upholds as constitutional the 1998 law that extended copyright terms by twenty years, even for works already published. Eric Eldred, a publisher of public-domain books on the internet, had sued with Lessig as counsel; Justices Stevens and Breyer dissented.

fuentes/fallo-eldred-contra-ashcroft/por.texto: The defeat led Lessig to promote the Creative Commons licenses and to write “Free Culture”.

fuentes/fallo-eldred-contra-ashcroft/lee.texto: Text of the ruling at Cornell's LII

fuentes/la-etica-del-hacker/titulo.texto: The Hacker Ethic and the Spirit of the Information Age

fuentes/la-etica-del-hacker/resumen.texto: Himanen contrasts the Protestant work ethic described by Max Weber (duty, discipline, schedule) with a hacker ethic based on passion, freedom to organize one's time and the social value of sharing. It has a prologue by Linus Torvalds and an epilogue by Manuel Castells.

fuentes/la-etica-del-hacker/por_que_impo.texto: It carried the idea of the “hacker” from computing into the sociology of work in the information society.

fuentes/hackers-levy/titulo.texto: Hackers: Heroes of the Computer Revolution

fuentes/hackers-levy/resumen.texto: Chronicle of three generations of hackers: those of the Tech Model Railroad Club and the MIT AI Lab in the 1950s and 1960s, the hardware hackers of the Homebrew Computer Club in California, and the game programmers of the 1980s. It ends with Richard Stallman as “the last of the true hackers”.

fuentes/hackers-levy/por_que_importa.texto: It systematized the “hacker ethic”: access to computers should be unlimited, all information should be free, mistrust authority and promote decentralization, and hackers should be judged by what they do and not by degrees, age or race.

fuentes/hackers-levy/leer.0.titulo.texto: Chapters 1 and 2, at Project Gutenberg with the author's permission

fuentes/jargon-file/autor.texto: Raphael Finkel, Eric S. Raymond and others

fuentes/jargon-file/resumen.texto: Glossary of hacker slang begun in 1975 at the Stanford AI Laboratory and expanded at MIT and other ARPANET sites; it was published in print as “The Hacker's Dictionary” (1983) and, edited by Eric Raymond from 1990, as “The New Hacker's Dictionary”. It defines a “hacker” as someone who enjoys exploring the details of systems and distinguishes the “cracker”, who breaks into other people's systems.

fuentes/jargon-file/por_que_importa.texto: It is a record of the community's culture and humor; Raymond's versions were criticized by old-time hackers for inserting his own opinions into it.

fuentes/manifiesto-hacker/titulo.texto: The Conscience of a Hacker (The Hacker Manifesto)

fuentes/manifiesto-hacker/soporte.texto: Text in the electronic magazine Phrack (issue 7)

fuentes/manifiesto-hacker/resumen.texto: Text written on 8 January 1986, shortly after its author was arrested, and published in September in Phrack. A teenager bored at school discovers the computer and networks, and answers those who call him a criminal: “my crime is that of curiosity”, that of judging people by what they say and think and not by what they look like.

fuentes/manifiesto-hacker/por_que_import.texto: It became the emblematic text of the 1980s hacker subculture and a defense of intrusion as exploration; its critics point out that it justifies entering other people's systems without permission.

fuentes/revista-2600/resumen.texto: Magazine founded in January 1984 by Eric Corley, whose name recalls the 2600-hertz frequency that “phreakers” used to control telephone exchanges. It publishes technical articles on security, telephony and surveillance, and letters from readers.

fuentes/revista-2600/por_que_importa.texto: It was the public voice of the American hacker community; in Universal v. Reimerdes (2000) a court barred it from publishing or linking to the DeCSS program under the DMCA.

fuentes/el-huevo-del-cuco/resumen.texto: Stoll recounts how a 75-cent discrepancy in the accounting of his laboratory's computers led him in 1986 to track down an intruder seeking military information on American networks. The trail ended in Hanover, with Markus Hess, part of a group of young West Germans who sold data to the KGB.

fuentes/el-huevo-del-cuco/por_que_import.texto: It is one of the first accounts of computer espionage and of how an intrusion is investigated; it showed how vulnerable academic and military networks were.

fuentes/analisis-del-gusano-de-internet/.texto: The Internet Worm Program: An Analysis

Report of 29 November 1988 describing step by step how Robert Morris's worm spread by exploiting flaws in the sendmail and fingerd programs and weak passwords, and why it multiplied far more than its author had anticipated.
It was the reference technical analysis of the first major internet security incident, which led to the creation of the first computer emergency response team (CERT).

fuentes/ley-cfaa/resumen.texto: 1986 federal law that punishes accessing computers “without authorization” or “exceeding authorized access”, with penalties that increase according to the damage. It was applied to Robert Morris, Kevin Mitnick, Aaron Swartz and Chelsea Manning, among others.

fuentes/ley-cfaa/por_que_importa.texto: Its critics fault its vagueness for allowing violations of a website's terms of use to be prosecuted as crimes; the Supreme Court narrowed it in Van Buren (2021).

fuentes/ley-cfaa/leer.0.titulo.texto: Current text (18 U.S.C. 1030) at Cornell's LII

fuentes/la-caza-de-hackers/resumen.texto: Chronicle of the 1990 police operations against hackers in the United States, including Operation Sundevil and the raid on Steve Jackson Games, following the crash of the AT&T telephone network in January of that year. It tells the history of telephony, of the phreakers, of the police and of the founders of the EFF.

fuentes/la-caza-de-hackers/por_que_impor.texto: It is the main source on the moment when law and civil rights reached the “electronic frontier”; Sterling released it free on the internet in 1994.

fuentes/la-caza-de-hackers/leer.0.titulo.texto: At Project Gutenberg, released by the author

fuentes/declaracion-de-independencia-del.texto: A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace

Text of 8 February 1996, written in Davos during the World Economic Forum in response to the United States Telecommunications Act, which sought to regulate “indecent” content on the internet. It addresses the “Governments of the Industrial World”: “you are not welcome among us”, and declares that cyberspace does not lie within their borders and will be governed by its own rules.
It expressed the cyberlibertarianism of the 1990s; Lessig and others objected that the internet is as regulable as any other space, through code and those who control it.

fuentes/la-economia-de-las-ideas/resumen.texto: Essay from March 1994 arguing that copyright, designed for physical “bottles” (books, records), does not work for digital information, which can be copied at no cost; it proposes that creators make a living from their relationship with their audience, performance and service.

fuentes/la-economia-de-las-ideas/por_que.texto: It anticipated the crisis of the record industry brought by digital copying and the debate over copyright on the internet.

fuentes/nuevas-direcciones-en-criptograf.texto: Article in IEEE Transactions on Information Theory

Article by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, from November 1976, proposing public-key cryptography: two parties can agree on a secret key over a public channel without having met, and documents can be signed digitally. It presents the key exchange that bears their names.
It made possible electronic commerce and encryption available to anyone; at the British GCHQ, Ellis, Cocks and Williamson had arrived earlier at similar ideas, but these were kept secret until 1997.

fuentes/articulo-rsa/titulo.texto: A Method for Obtaining Digital Signatures and Public-Key Cryptosystems

fuentes/articulo-rsa/soporte.texto: Article in Communications of the ACM

fuentes/articulo-rsa/resumen.texto: Article by Rivest, Shamir and Adleman presenting the RSA algorithm, based on the difficulty of factoring the product of two large prime numbers. It circulated as an MIT memo in 1977, was publicized by Martin Gardner in Scientific American and was published in February 1978.

fuentes/articulo-rsa/por_que_importa.texto: RSA was the first practical public-key and digital signature system; its patent, from 1983, expired in 2000.

fuentes/seguridad-sin-identificacion/sop.texto: Article in Communications of the ACM

fuentes/seguridad-sin-identificacion/res.texto: Article from October 1985 warning that the computerization of payments and transactions makes it possible to compile profiles of each person, and proposing cryptographic systems (blind signatures, pseudonyms) to carry out verifiable transactions without revealing identity.

fuentes/seguridad-sin-identificacion/por.texto: It is the theoretical basis of anonymous electronic cash and a direct inspiration for the cypherpunks and cryptocurrencies.

fuentes/seguridad-sin-identificacion/lee.texto: Chaum's article (1985), copy from Radboud University

fuentes/manifiesto-criptoanarquista/sopo.texto: Short text, circulated in 1992 on the cypherpunk mailing list

fuentes/manifiesto-criptoanarquista/resu.texto: Text from 1988 announcing that cryptography will allow individuals and groups to communicate and trade anonymously, which will change the nature of state regulation, taxation and trade secrets. “A specter is haunting the modern world, the specter of crypto anarchy”.

fuentes/manifiesto-criptoanarquista/por_.texto: It stated bluntly that encryption would weaken the state; the cypherpunks took it as a program and its critics as an invitation to evasion and crime.

fuentes/manifiesto-cypherpunk/resumen.texto: Text of 9 March 1993 that defines privacy as “the power to selectively reveal oneself to the world” and distinguishes it from secrecy. It argues that governments and corporations cannot be expected to grant it and that it must be defended with cryptography: “cypherpunks write code”.

fuentes/manifiesto-cypherpunk/por_que_im.texto: It is the statement of principles of the cypherpunk movement, which gave rise to PGP, anonymous remailers, Bitcoin and WikiLeaks.

fuentes/por-que-escribi-pgp/resumen.texto: Text from 1991, updated in 1999, in which Zimmermann explains that he released his encryption program for free in response to a Senate bill that would have required manufacturers of communications equipment to allow the government to read messages. He argues that in the digital age privacy depends on encryption and that “if privacy is outlawed, only outlaws will have privacy”.

fuentes/por-que-escribi-pgp/por_que_impo.texto: It explains the gesture that brought strong encryption to the public and triggered the criminal investigation of its author for exporting munitions.

fuentes/fallo-bernstein/titulo.texto: Bernstein v. United States Department of Justice

fuentes/fallo-bernstein/autor.texto: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit

fuentes/fallo-bernstein/resumen.texto: Ruling of 6 May 1999 confirming that cryptography export rules violated freedom of speech by requiring prior permission to publish the source code of an encryption program. The student Daniel Bernstein had sued in 1995 with the support of the EFF; the court later vacated the ruling to rehear it en banc, and the government changed the rules in 2000.

fuentes/fallo-bernstein/por_que_importa.texto: It established in case law the idea that source code is a form of expression, central to the “crypto wars”.

fuentes/fallo-bernstein/leer.0.titulo.texto: Case documents on the EFF website

fuentes/bitcoin-whitepaper/titulo.texto: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System

fuentes/bitcoin-whitepaper/resumen.texto: Paper circulated on 31 October 2008 on a cryptography mailing list, in the midst of the financial crisis, proposing electronic cash without banks or intermediaries: transactions are recorded in a public blockchain and ordered by “proof of work”, which prevents spending the same coin twice.

fuentes/bitcoin-whitepaper/por_que_impor.texto: It solved the double-spending problem without a central authority and gave rise to cryptocurrencies; its supporters see it as money free from state control, its critics point to speculation, energy consumption and its use in crime.

fuentes/whitepaper-ethereum/titulo.texto: Ethereum: A Next-Generation Smart Contract and Decentralized Application Platform

fuentes/whitepaper-ethereum/resumen.texto: Paper from late 2013 in which Buterin, then 19 years old, proposes a blockchain with a complete programming language, to record not only payments but programs (“smart contracts”) that execute themselves: decentralized currencies, organizations and markets.

fuentes/whitepaper-ethereum/por_que_impo.texto: It is the basis of Ethereum, launched in 2015, and of a large share of later cryptocurrency applications.

fuentes/libre-como-en-libertad/titulo.texto: Free as in Freedom: Richard Stallman's Crusade for Free Software

fuentes/libre-como-en-libertad/resumen.texto: Biography of Stallman based on interviews with him and with people who worked with him: his childhood, the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, the episode of the Xerox printer whose code he was not allowed to modify, the GNU Project and the dispute with open source.

fuentes/libre-como-en-libertad/por_que_i.texto: It was published under the GNU Free Documentation License; in 2010 Stallman revised and corrected a second edition together with the author.

fuentes/libre-como-en-libertad/leer.0.ti.texto: Full text at O'Reilly, under a free license

fuentes/conspiracion-como-gobernanza/sop.texto: Essay published on the author's website

fuentes/conspiracion-como-gobernanza/res.texto: Essay from December 2006 that describes authoritarian governments and other organizations as “conspiracies”: networks that depend on communicating in secret. If leaking their communications makes that secrecy more costly, the conspiracy becomes clumsy and less able to act.

fuentes/conspiracion-como-gobernanza/por.texto: It is the theory Assange used to justify WikiLeaks: leaking not only informs but forces opaque organizations to change.

fuentes/conspiracion-como-gobernanza/lee.texto: Copy of the author's website on the Internet Archive

fuentes/cypherpunks-libro/titulo.texto: Cypherpunks: Freedom and the Future of the Internet

fuentes/cypherpunks-libro/resumen.texto: Conversation between Julian Assange, Jacob Appelbaum, Andy Müller-Maguhn and Jérémie Zimmermann, recorded in 2012 for Assange's television show. They argue that the internet has become a tool of mass surveillance serving states and corporations, and that cryptography is citizens' defense.

fuentes/cypherpunks-libro/por_que_import.texto: It sums up WikiLeaks' political vision a year before Snowden's revelations, which confirmed some of its claims.

fuentes/fallo-new-york-times-contra-esta.texto: New York Times Co. v. United States
Supreme Court of the United States

Ruling of June 30, 1971 that, by six votes to three, rejects the Nixon administration's request to bar The New York Times and The Washington Post from publishing the Pentagon Papers: prior restraint requires a very strong justification, which the government did not demonstrate.

It is the precedent that protects media outlets that publish secret information; it did not settle whether the person who leaks it can be prosecuted, the question at stake in the cases of Manning, Snowden and Assange.
Text of the ruling at Cornell's LII

fuentes/ley-de-espionaje/resumen.texto: Law enacted on June 15, 1917, during the First World War, that punishes obtaining or transmitting national defense information with intent or reason to believe that it will be used to the injury of the United States or to the advantage of a foreign nation. It does not admit the public interest of what was revealed as a defense.

fuentes/ley-de-espionaje/por_que_importa.texto: It was used against Daniel Ellsberg, Chelsea Manning, Edward Snowden and, for the first time against a publisher, against Julian Assange; its critics say it prevents whistleblowers from defending themselves.

fuentes/wikileaks-la-guerra-de-assange/t.texto: WikiLeaks: Inside Julian Assange's War on Secrecy

fuentes/wikileaks-la-guerra-de-assange/r.texto: Account by two Guardian journalists of the newspaper's collaboration with WikiLeaks in 2010 and its break with Assange. It included the password to the full archive of the cables, which Leigh believed had expired; when the unredacted archive circulated in 2011, the newspaper and WikiLeaks blamed each other.

fuentes/wikileaks-la-guerra-de-assange/p.texto: It is the account of one of the partner media outlets and a central source on the criticism of Assange; WikiLeaks rejects it.

fuentes/articulo-verizon/titulo.texto: NSA collecting phone records of millions of Verizon customers daily

fuentes/articulo-verizon/resumen.texto: First story based on Snowden's documents, published on June 5, 2013: a secret order from the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court required the company Verizon to hand over to the NSA the metadata of all its customers' calls. The next day The Guardian and The Washington Post revealed the PRISM program.

fuentes/articulo-verizon/por_que_importa.texto: It started the 2013 series of revelations and the worldwide debate on mass surveillance.

fuentes/sin-lugar-donde-esconderse/resum.texto: Greenwald recounts his contact with Snowden, the meeting in Hong Kong and the publication of the first stories, and reproduces documents on mass data collection. He criticizes the press that, in his view, subordinated itself to the government.

fuentes/sin-lugar-donde-esconderse/por_q.texto: It is the account of the journalist at the center of events; his critics fault him for taking his source's side.

fuentes/vigilancia-permanente/resumen.texto: Snowden's memoir: his upbringing, his work for the CIA and the NSA, how he concluded that mass surveillance violated the Constitution, and how he gathered and handed over the documents. He argues that he acted as a whistleblower because internal channels did not protect contractors.

fuentes/vigilancia-permanente/por_que_im.texto: On the day of its publication the United States government sued him for not having submitted the text to the prepublication review he was bound by; a judge sided with the government and ordered him to hand over the proceeds.

fuentes/fallo-aclu-contra-clapper/autor.texto: Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit

fuentes/fallo-aclu-contra-clapper/resume.texto: Ruling of May 7, 2015 holding that the bulk collection of telephone records revealed by Snowden exceeded what Section 215 of the Patriot Act authorized. It did not rule on its constitutionality.

fuentes/fallo-aclu-contra-clapper/por_qu.texto: It was the first appeals court to find the program illegal; Congress replaced it weeks later with the USA Freedom Act.

fuentes/usa-freedom-act/resumen.texto: Law of June 2, 2015 that ends the NSA's bulk collection of telephone records: the data stay with the companies and the government must request those of specific targets with a court order. It adds an advocate before the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court and more transparency.

fuentes/usa-freedom-act/por_que_importa.texto: It was the main legal reform resulting from Snowden's revelations; for some it was a step forward, for others a minimal reform that left other programs in place.

fuentes/informe-del-congreso-sobre-snowd.texto: House Intelligence Committee report on Snowden
House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence
Congressional report (declassified and redacted version, December 2016)

Report approved unanimously in September 2016 arguing that Snowden was not a whistleblower, because he did not use legal channels, that most of what he took concerned not surveillance programs but defense and military intelligence, and that he caused tremendous damage to national security.
It is Congress's official position on Snowden; he and journalists who covered him called it misleading and disputed several of its claims.

fuentes/fallo-extradicion-de-assange/res.texto: Ruling of January 4, 2021 that rejects Assange's arguments that the United States' request was political and violated freedom of expression, but denies extradition because, given his mental health, the risk of suicide in a US prison would be very high.

fuentes/fallo-extradicion-de-assange/por.texto: The High Court overturned it in December 2021 after US assurances about his treatment; in 2024 it allowed him to appeal on free speech grounds, and the case ended with a deal before that appeal.

fuentes/fallo-extradicion-de-assange/lee.texto: Text of the ruling on the UK Judiciary website

fuentes/investigacion-papeles-de-panama/.texto: International Consortium of Investigative Journalists and Süddeutsche Zeitung

Investigation published from April 3, 2016 by more than a hundred media outlets based on 11.5 million documents from the Panamanian law firm Mossack Fonseca, handed to the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung by an anonymous source. It exposed offshore companies belonging to politicians, businesspeople and athletes from dozens of countries.

It led to the resignation of Iceland's prime minister, tax investigations in many countries and the closure of the firm in 2018; it showed the scale that collaborative journalism based on leaks could reach.
The investigation on the ICIJ website

fuentes/mensaje-a-la-cienciologia/resume.texto: Video of January 21, 2008, with a synthetic voice over images of clouds, in which Anonymous declares war on the Church of Scientology for trying to remove an internal video of Tom Cruise from the internet, and announces that it will “expel it from the internet”. It ends with the motto “We are Anonymous. We are Legion. We do not forgive. We do not forget. Expect us”.

fuentes/mensaje-a-la-cienciologia/por_qu.texto: It marked Anonymous's shift from forum pranks to political action, with the street protests of February 2008.

fuentes/manifiesto-guerrilla-del-acceso-.texto: Text from July 2008 denouncing that scientific knowledge, largely funded with public money, is locked up by publishers that charge to read it. It calls on those who have access (students, librarians, scientists) to download and share those articles, even if it means breaking contracts: “there is no justice in following unjust laws”.
It was read as the program behind the mass JSTOR downloads for which Swartz was prosecuted, and became a central text of the open access movement.

fuentes/declaracion-de-budapest/autor.texto: Budapest meeting of the Open Society Institute

fuentes/declaracion-de-budapest/resumen.texto: Declaration of February 14, 2002, arising from a meeting convened by George Soros's Open Society Institute, that defines “open access” to scientific literature: freely available on the internet, with permission to read, copy, distribute and use it. It proposes two routes: self-archiving in repositories and open access journals.

fuentes/declaracion-de-budapest/por_que_.texto: It is the founding text of the open access movement, adopted by universities and funding bodies around the world.

fuentes/declaracion-de-berlin/autor.texto: Max Planck Society and other institutions

fuentes/declaracion-de-berlin/resumen.texto: Declaration of October 22, 2003, promoted by the Max Planck Society, in which scientific institutions commit to promoting open access to research results and to cultural heritage, including data and images.

fuentes/declaracion-de-berlin/por_que_im.texto: Signed by hundreds of universities and academies, it brought open access into European science policy.

fuentes/citizenfour/resumen.texto: Documentary filmed largely in the Hong Kong hotel room where, in June 2013, Snowden met for eight days with Laura Poitras, Glenn Greenwald and Ewen MacAskill to hand them the documents. It shows the preparation of the first stories and Snowden's decision to reveal his identity.

fuentes/citizenfour/por_que_importa.texto: It is the direct record of the moment of the leak; it won the Oscar for Best Documentary in 2015.

fuentes/readme-txt/resumen.texto: Manning's memoir: her childhood in Oklahoma and Wales, her enlistment in the Army, her work as an analyst in Iraq, why she handed the documents to WikiLeaks, her detention in Kuwait and at Quantico, the court-martial, her gender transition in prison and her renewed imprisonment in 2019 for refusing to testify before a grand jury about WikiLeaks.

fuentes/readme-txt/por_que_importa.texto: It is the leaker's account of her motives, which she presents as the wish for the public to know the real cost of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

fuentes/hacker-hoaxer/titulo.texto: Hacker, Hoaxer, Whistleblower, Spy: The Many Faces of Anonymous

fuentes/hacker-hoaxer/resumen.texto: Study by anthropologist Gabriella Coleman, who followed Anonymous's chat channels for years: how it went from 4chan pranks to campaigns against Scientology and in support of WikiLeaks and the Arab Spring, and how LulzSec ended with its members arrested.

fuentes/hacker-hoaxer/por_que_importa.texto: It is the reference study on Anonymous, which the author describes as a collective without leaders or a fixed ideology that organizes itself through operations.

fuentes/el-futuro-de-las-ideas/titulo.texto: The Future of Ideas: The Fate of the Commons in a Connected World

fuentes/el-futuro-de-las-ideas/resumen.texto: Lessig, then a law professor at Stanford and a critic of the extension of copyright terms in the United States, continues *Code*. He warns that an overly strict and long intellectual property regime can stifle innovation, because the future is always built on the past, and he analyzes companies’ attempts to protect more, and for longer, three layers of the Internet: the code layer (software), the content layer (the Napster case and the reaction of the music and film industries) and the physical layer (the radio spectrum). He argues that existing works should pass into the public domain within a reasonable period, as the Founding Fathers intended.

fuentes/el-futuro-de-las-ideas/por_que_i.texto: It lays the groundwork for the argument of Free Culture (2004) and the founding of Creative Commons. In 2008 Lessig announced that the publishers had agreed to license the book under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial.

fuentes/el-futuro-de-las-ideas/leer.0.ti.texto: Free edition (Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 3.0) on the Internet Archive, in PDF and epub

fuentes/just-for-fun/titulo.texto: Just for Fun: The Story of an Accidental Revolutionary

fuentes/just-for-fun/soporte.texto: Book (autobiography written with David Diamond; HarperCollins)

fuentes/just-for-fun/resumen.texto: A humorous autobiography by Linus Torvalds, written with the journalist David Diamond. It tells how he himself sees the free software movement and the development of Linux, and how a system that began as a hobby came to be used far more widely than anyone expected.

fuentes/just-for-fun/por_que_importa.texto: It is the author’s own account of the origins of Linux, complementing his 1991 announcement and his dispute with Tanenbaum.

fuentes/arte-de-programar-unix/resumen.texto: History and culture of UNIX programming from its beginnings in 1969 to 2003, covering both its genetic offshoots (BSD) and its conceptual ones (Linux). It compares UNIX with other systems, such as Microsoft Windows and classic Mac OS, or Bell Labs’ EROS and Plan 9, and includes contributions and comments from UNIX figures such as Ken Thompson, Brian Kernighan, Doug McIlroy and Henry Spencer.

fuentes/arte-de-programar-unix/por_que_i.texto: It extends to the whole engineering culture of UNIX what Raymond had set out in “The Cathedral and the Bazaar” (1997). It is available online under a Creative Commons license with additional terms.

fuentes/arte-de-programar-unix/leer.0.ti.texto: Full text on Eric Raymond’s site (Creative Commons license with additional terms)

personas/stallman/resumen.texto: Programmer at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory who launched the GNU Project in 1983 and founded the Free Software Foundation in 1985. He formulated the idea of free software, wrote the GPL license and maintains that proprietary software is an injustice; in 2019 he resigned as president of the FSF after a controversy over comments about the Epstein case and returned to its board in 2021.

personas/torvalds/resumen.texto: Finnish programmer who in 1991, as a student in Helsinki, wrote the Linux kernel and published it on the internet. Since 1992 he has distributed it under the GPL and still coordinates its development; he describes himself as a pragmatist and is wary of free software activism.

personas/eric-raymond/resumen.texto: American programmer and essayist, author of “The Cathedral and the Bazaar” (1997) and editor of the Jargon File. In 1998 he co-founded the Open Source Initiative and promoted the term “open source” as a more business-friendly alternative to Stallman's “free software”.

personas/bruce-perens/resumen.texto: American programmer who, as Debian project leader, drafted in 1997 its Social Contract and the Debian Free Software Guidelines, from which the Open Source Definition was derived; he co-founded the OSI with Raymond in 1998.

personas/ian-murdock/resumen.texto: Founder of Debian (1993), whose name combines his own with that of his then-girlfriend Debra; he wrote the Debian Manifesto as a student at Purdue University. He died in San Francisco in 2015.

personas/eben-moglen/resumen.texto: Law professor at Columbia University and legal counsel to the Free Software Foundation; he drafted GPL version 3 (2007) with Stallman and founded the Software Freedom Law Center.

personas/andrew-tanenbaum/resumen.texto: Professor at the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, author of MINIX, the teaching operating system that inspired Linux. In 1992 he debated Torvalds over the design of the kernel.

personas/pekka-himanen/resumen.texto: Finnish philosopher, author of “The Hacker Ethic and the Spirit of the Information Age” (2001), which contrasts the hacker work ethic with the Protestant ethic described by Max Weber.

personas/steven-levy/resumen.texto: American technology journalist, author of “Hackers” (1984), in which he systematized the “hacker ethic”, and of “Crypto” (2001), on civilian cryptography.

personas/lawrence-lessig/resumen.texto: American legal scholar, professor at Stanford and Harvard, author of “Code” (1999) and “Free Culture” (2004). He co-founded Creative Commons in 2001 and argued Eldred v. Ashcroft before the Supreme Court, which he lost.

personas/jimmy-wales/resumen.texto: American entrepreneur who founded Wikipedia in 2001 together with Larry Sanger and created the Wikimedia Foundation in 2003, which supports it through donations.

personas/larry-sanger/resumen.texto: American philosopher, co-founder of Wikipedia in 2001, from which he distanced himself in 2002; he later criticized it for its lack of rigor and for what he considers an ideological bias.

personas/brewster-kahle/resumen.texto: American computer scientist who founded the Internet Archive in 1996, with the goal of providing “universal access to all knowledge”.

personas/bill-gates/resumen.texto: Co-founder of Microsoft (1975) with Paul Allen. In 1976 he wrote the “Open Letter to Hobbyists”, against the unauthorized copying of software; with MS-DOS and Windows, Microsoft dominated the personal computer market. Since 2008 he has devoted himself mainly to his philanthropic foundation.

personas/paul-allen/resumen.texto: Co-founder of Microsoft with Bill Gates, with whom he wrote BASIC for the Altair 8800 in 1975; he left the company in 1983.

personas/steve-ballmer/resumen.texto: CEO of Microsoft from 2000 to 2014. In 2001 he called Linux “a cancer” because of the GPL's effect on intellectual property. His successor, Satya Nadella, proclaimed in 2014 that Microsoft “loves Linux”.

personas/craig-mundie/resumen.texto: Microsoft executive who in 2001 defended the “commercial software model” against the GPL and presented the “shared source” initiative.

personas/steve-jobs/resumen.texto: Co-founder of Apple (1976) with Steve Wozniak, driving force behind the Macintosh, the iPod and the iPhone. Apple combined closed systems with free foundations: its macOS relies on Darwin, derived from BSD.

personas/thomas-penfield-jackson/resumen.texto: Federal judge in Washington who in 2000 ruled that Microsoft had abused its monopoly and ordered it broken up. The Court of Appeals overturned the breakup in 2001 and removed him from the case for having spoken with journalists during the trial.

personas/the-mentor/resumen.texto: American hacker of the Legion of Doom group who, under the pseudonym “The Mentor”, wrote “The Conscience of a Hacker” in 1986, known as the Hacker Manifesto. He was working at Steve Jackson Games when the Secret Service raided the company in 1990.

personas/wau-holland/resumen.texto: German journalist, co-founder of the Chaos Computer Club in 1981, which he turned into a public voice on freedom of information and privacy. The foundation that bears his name raised donations for WikiLeaks.

personas/eric-corley/resumen.texto: Editor of the magazine 2600 since 1984, under the pseudonym “Emmanuel Goldstein”, taken from Orwell's “1984”. He led the “Free Kevin” campaign for Kevin Mitnick and organizes the HOPE conferences.

personas/kevin-mitnick/resumen.texto: American hacker, famous for social engineering, who in the 1980s and 1990s broke into the systems of telephone and computer companies. He was arrested in 1995 after years as a fugitive, spent almost five years in prison and later worked as a security consultant.

personas/robert-tappan-morris/resumen.texto: Cornell University student who in 1988 released the Morris worm, one of the first to spread across the internet. He was the first person convicted under the federal computer fraud law; he later became a professor at MIT.

personas/clifford-stoll/resumen.texto: Astronomer at the Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory who in 1986 traced a computer intruder to a ring of West German hackers who were selling information to the KGB; he told the story in “The Cuckoo's Egg” (1989).

personas/bruce-sterling/resumen.texto: Cyberpunk science fiction writer and journalist, author of “The Hacker Crackdown” (1992), which he released for free on the internet.

personas/mitch-kapor/resumen.texto: Founder of the software company Lotus and co-founder of the Electronic Frontier Foundation (1990), with John Perry Barlow and John Gilmore.

personas/christopher-poole/resumen.texto: Creator in 2003, as a teenager and under the pseudonym “moot”, of the anonymous image board 4chan, where Anonymous emerged.

personas/hector-monsegur/resumen.texto: New York hacker, leader of LulzSec under the pseudonym “Sabu”. Secretly arrested in June 2011, he cooperated with the FBI to identify other members; in 2014 he was sentenced to time served.

personas/diffie/resumen.texto: American cryptographer who, with Martin Hellman, published the idea of public-key cryptography in 1976. Turing Award 2015.

personas/hellman/resumen.texto: Stanford professor, co-author with Diffie of “New Directions in Cryptography” (1976), which opened cryptography to the civilian sphere against the monopoly of intelligence agencies.

personas/rivest/resumen.texto: MIT professor, the R in the RSA algorithm (1977), created with Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman.

personas/shamir/resumen.texto: Israeli cryptographer, the S in RSA, later a professor at the Weizmann Institute.

personas/adleman/resumen.texto: American computer scientist, the A in RSA; later a pioneer of DNA computing.

personas/david-chaum/resumen.texto: American cryptographer who from 1981 onward proposed anonymous mail networks and anonymous electronic cash; his company DigiCash (1990) was a precursor of cryptocurrencies.

personas/phil-zimmermann/resumen.texto: American programmer who in 1991 released PGP, a free email encryption program. He was investigated from 1993 to 1996 for exporting cryptography without a license, without being charged.

personas/tim-may/resumen.texto: Intel engineer who wrote “The Crypto Anarchist Manifesto” (1988) and co-founded the cypherpunk mailing list in 1992.

personas/eric-hughes/resumen.texto: American mathematician, co-founder of the cypherpunk list in 1992 and author of “A Cypherpunk's Manifesto” (1993).

personas/john-gilmore/resumen.texto: One of the first employees of Sun Microsystems, co-founder of the EFF (1990), the cypherpunk list (1992) and the free software company Cygnus Solutions.

personas/john-perry-barlow/resumen.texto: Grateful Dead lyricist and Wyoming rancher, co-founder of the EFF (1990). In 1996, in Davos, he wrote the “Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace”.

personas/satoshi-nakamoto/resumen.texto: Pseudonym of the person or group that published the Bitcoin paper in 2008 and launched the network in 2009. They stopped participating in 2010-2011; their identity remains unknown.

personas/hal-finney/resumen.texto: PGP programmer and cypherpunk who received the first bitcoin transaction, sent by Satoshi Nakamoto in January 2009.

personas/vitalik-buterin/resumen.texto: Russian-Canadian programmer who in 2013 proposed Ethereum, a blockchain for running programs (“smart contracts”), launched in 2015.

personas/ross-ulbricht/resumen.texto: Creator of Silk Road, an anonymous marketplace on the Tor network that operated with bitcoin. Sentenced in 2015 to life in prison for drug trafficking, money laundering and computer crimes, he was pardoned by Donald Trump in January 2025.

personas/assange/resumen.texto: Australian programmer and activist who founded WikiLeaks in 2006. His supporters see him as a journalist persecuted for publishing war crimes; the United States accused him of conspiring with Chelsea Manning to obtain and disclose secrets. After seven years in the Ecuadorian embassy and five in Belmarsh prison, in 2024 he pleaded guilty to one charge and was freed.

personas/chelsea-manning/resumen.texto: United States Army intelligence analyst who in 2010 handed WikiLeaks hundreds of thousands of military and diplomatic documents. A court-martial sentenced her in 2013 to 35 years; Obama commuted the sentence in 2017.

personas/snowden/resumen.texto: NSA contractor who in 2013 gave journalists documents on the mass surveillance programs of the United States and its allies. Charged in his country with theft and violating the Espionage Act, he lives in Russia, which granted him citizenship in 2022.

personas/daniel-ellsberg/resumen.texto: Military analyst who in 1971 gave the press the Pentagon Papers on the Vietnam War. His espionage trial was dismissed in 1973 because of the government's illegal conduct; he later defended Manning and Snowden.

personas/glenn-greenwald/resumen.texto: American journalist and lawyer who published in The Guardian, in 2013, the first articles based on Snowden's documents; he lives in Brazil.

personas/laura-poitras/resumen.texto: American documentary filmmaker whom Snowden contacted first; she filmed his interviews in Hong Kong for “Citizenfour” (2014), which won the Oscar for best documentary.

personas/aaron-swartz/resumen.texto: American programmer and activist who took part in creating the RSS format, the Creative Commons licenses and Reddit. Charged for mass-downloading JSTOR articles from the MIT network, he took his own life in 2013 before trial.

personas/alexandra-elbakyan/resumen.texto: Kazakh programmer who in 2011 created Sci-Hub to get around the fees charged by scientific publishers. United States courts ordered her by default to pay millions in damages for copyright infringement.

personas/peter-sunde/resumen.texto: Spokesperson for The Pirate Bay, convicted in Sweden in 2009 (and on appeal in 2010) of complicity in copyright infringement; he served five months in prison in 2014.

personas/rick-falkvinge/resumen.texto: Swedish IT entrepreneur who founded the Pirate Party in 2006 to reform copyright and patent law and protect privacy.

hechos/hackers-del-tmrc/titulo.texto: The hackers of the Tech Model Railroad Club

hechos/hackers-del-tmrc/resumen.texto: Students from MIT's model railroad club, who called an ingenious solution a “hack,” began programming the TX-0 and PDP-1 computers at night. From that milieu, which moved on to the AI Lab, came the word “hacker” and the custom of sharing code.

hechos/spacewar/resumen.texto: Steve Russell and other MIT hackers programmed one of the first video games, a spaceship duel for the PDP-1 computer. It circulated freely, with its code, among the universities that had that machine.

hechos/homebrew-computer-club/resumen.texto: Club of microcomputer hobbyists founded in March 1975, where circuits and programs were exchanged; Steve Wozniak and Steve Jobs came out of it. The copying of Microsoft's Altair BASIC at its meetings prompted Bill Gates's 1976 open letter.

hechos/fundacion-de-microsoft/resumen.texto: Bill Gates and Paul Allen founded Micro-Soft in Albuquerque to sell a BASIC interpreter for the Altair 8800. In 1979 it moved to the Seattle area and in 1986 to Redmond.

hechos/fundacion-de-apple/resumen.texto: Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne founded Apple Computer on April 1, 1976 to sell the Apple I computer, built by Wozniak.

hechos/ibm-pc-y-ms-dos/resumen.texto: IBM launched its personal computer in August 1981 with an operating system that Microsoft licensed to it non-exclusively. When other manufacturers copied the PC architecture, Microsoft sold them the same system, MS-DOS, and took over the industry standard.

hechos/proyecto-gnu/resumen.texto: Richard Stallman announced on September 27, 1983 that he would write GNU, a free Unix-compatible operating system, and in January 1984 he left his job at MIT so that the university could not claim the code. In the following years he wrote the Emacs editor and the GCC compiler.

hechos/fundacion-del-chaos-computer-club.texto: Founding of the Chaos Computer Club

Wau Holland and others founded Europe's largest hacker club on September 12, 1981, in the offices of the Berlin newspaper taz. In 1984 it became known for exposing flaws in the postal service's Btx system by transferring, and returning, 134,000 marks from a Hamburg savings bank.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-fsf/titulo.texto: Founding of the Free Software Foundation

hechos/fundacion-de-la-fsf/resumen.texto: Stallman founded the Free Software Foundation on October 4, 1985, a nonprofit organization that funds the GNU Project, administers the GPL and promotes the idea of free software.

hechos/caso-hess/titulo.texto: The Hanover hackers and the KGB

hechos/caso-hess/resumen.texto: Clifford Stoll discovered from Berkeley that an intruder, Markus Hess, was breaking into US military networks. Hess and other young West Germans were selling what they obtained to the KGB; they were tried in 1990 and given suspended sentences.

hechos/gusano-morris/resumen.texto: On November 2, 1988 a program by Robert Tappan Morris, launched from MIT, copied itself onto thousands of internet computers and overloaded them. Morris said he only wanted to measure the network; in 1990 he was sentenced to three years' probation, community service and a fine.

hechos/operacion-sundevil/titulo.texto: Operation Sundevil and the raid on Steve Jackson Games

hechos/operacion-sundevil/resumen.texto: In May 1990 the Secret Service raided suspected hackers in fourteen cities, after having raided the game publisher Steve Jackson Games in March. In 1993 a court ordered the Secret Service to pay damages to the publisher for violating the laws protecting publications and stored communications.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-eff/titulo.texto: Founding of the Electronic Frontier Foundation

hechos/fundacion-de-la-eff/resumen.texto: Mitch Kapor, John Perry Barlow and John Gilmore founded the EFF in July 1990 to defend civil rights online, prompted by that year's raids. It backed the Steve Jackson Games and Bernstein cases.

hechos/creacion-de-linux/resumen.texto: Linus Torvalds released the first version of the Linux kernel in September 1991 and adopted the GPL license in 1992. Combined with the GNU tools it formed a complete free operating system; the FSF asks that it be called GNU/Linux.

hechos/pgp-y-la-investigacion-a-zimmerma.texto: PGP and the investigation of Zimmermann

Phil Zimmermann released PGP in 1991, and it spread over the internet outside the United States. Because strong cryptography was on the munitions list, the Customs Service investigated him from 1993 for illegal export; in 1995 MIT published the code as a printed book, protected by freedom of speech, and in 1996 prosecutors closed the case without charging him.

hechos/lista-cypherpunk/titulo.texto: The cypherpunk mailing list is born

hechos/lista-cypherpunk/resumen.texto: Eric Hughes, Timothy May and John Gilmore brought together a group of cryptographers and programmers in late 1992 and started a mailing list that grew to hundreds of members. They advocated privacy through encryption and anonymous digital cash.

hechos/chip-clipper/resumen.texto: Bill Clinton's administration proposed in 1993 an encryption chip for telephones whose keys would be held in escrow so that agencies could decrypt with a court order. Industry and privacy advocates rejected it; in 1994 Matt Blaze showed a flaw that allowed the escrow to be bypassed, and the project was abandoned around 1996.

hechos/guerras-criptograficas/resumen.texto: Dispute between the United States government, which treated cryptography as a munition and sought access to encrypted communications, and companies, academics and cypherpunks who defended free encryption. It ended in January 2000 with the liberalization of exports, although the debate over law-enforcement access later returned.

hechos/fundacion-de-debian/resumen.texto: Ian Murdock announced Debian on August 16, 1993, a GNU/Linux distribution made by volunteers. With its social contract and free software guidelines it became one of the most influential distributions, the basis of Ubuntu and many others.

hechos/apache/resumen.texto: A group of site administrators combined patches for the NCSA web server in 1995 and formed the Apache server, with free code, which within a few years became the most widely used on the web. The Apache Software Foundation was created in 1999.

hechos/netscape-libera-su-codigo/titulo.texto: Netscape releases its browser's source code

hechos/netscape-libera-su-codigo/resumen.texto: Netscape, which was losing the browser war with Microsoft, announced in January 1998 that it would release its browser's source code, and published it on March 31 as the Mozilla project, from which Firefox emerged in 2004.

hechos/nacimiento-del-codigo-abierto/tit.texto: Birth of “open source” and the Open Source Initiative

hechos/nacimiento-del-codigo-abierto/res.texto: In February 1998, following Netscape's announcement, Christine Peterson proposed the term “open source” to present free software to businesses without Stallman's ethical emphasis. Eric Raymond and Bruce Perens founded the Open Source Initiative. The FSF maintains that the change of name obscured the question of freedom.

hechos/juicio-antimonopolio-a-microsoft/.texto: United States v. Microsoft antitrust case

The Department of Justice and twenty states sued Microsoft in 1998 for using its Windows monopoly to push out Netscape. Judge Jackson ordered the company broken up in 2000; the Court of Appeals upheld the monopoly abuse finding in 2001 but overturned the breakup, and the case ended in a settlement approved in 2002.

hechos/fundacion-de-wikipedia/resumen.texto: Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger launched on January 15, 2001 an encyclopedia that anyone could edit, as a complement to Nupedia. With free licenses and volunteer work, it became one of the most widely used reference works in the world; since 2003 it has been supported by the Wikimedia Foundation.

hechos/fundacion-de-creative-commons/res.texto: Lawrence Lessig, Hal Abelson and Eric Eldred founded in 2001 an organization to make it easier for authors to share their works under standard licenses; the first ones were published in December 2002.

hechos/fundacion-de-the-pirate-bay/resum.texto: The Swedish group Piratbyrån, opposed to copyright, created in 2003 a BitTorrent file search engine that became the best known in the world. Swedish police raided it in 2006, which spurred the founding of the Pirate Party.

hechos/juicio-de-the-pirate-bay/resumen.texto: On April 17, 2009 a Stockholm court convicted four people responsible for the site of complicity in copyright infringement, sentencing them to one year in prison and to pay damages to record labels and studios. In 2010 the appeal reduced the prison sentences and increased the damages; the defendants argued that the site only indexed files.

hechos/fundacion-del-partido-pirata/titu.texto: Founding of the Swedish Pirate Party

hechos/fundacion-del-partido-pirata/resu.texto: Rick Falkvinge founded on January 1, 2006 a party to reform copyright and patent law and defend privacy. In the 2009 European elections it won 7.1% of the vote and one seat, later joined by another, and its example was copied in dozens of countries.

hechos/fundacion-de-4chan/titulo.texto: Founding of 4chan and the origin of Anonymous

hechos/fundacion-de-4chan/resumen.texto: Christopher Poole opened the image board 4chan in October 2003, where posts were signed “Anonymous” by default. From that custom and the forum's collective pranks emerged the identity of Anonymous.

hechos/proyecto-chanology/lugar.texto: Internet and outside Church of Scientology centers

hechos/proyecto-chanology/resumen.texto: Anonymous campaign against the Church of Scientology, begun in January 2008 after the Church tried to remove a Tom Cruise video from the internet. It combined attacks on its websites with street protests in Guy Fawkes masks outside its centers in dozens of cities on February 10, 2008.

hechos/papeles-del-pentagono-en-la-prens.texto: The publication of the Pentagon Papers

On June 13, 1971 The New York Times began publishing the secret study on Vietnam that Daniel Ellsberg had given it. The Nixon administration obtained a halt to publication, but the Supreme Court allowed it on June 30; the espionage case against Ellsberg was dismissed in 1973 when wiretaps and a break-in ordered against him from the White House came to light.

hechos/fundacion-de-wikileaks/resumen.texto: Julian Assange and a group of collaborators created in 2006 a website to receive and publish leaked documents while protecting the identity of sources; its first publication, in December, was a document about Somalia. In its early years it released Guantánamo manuals and documents on corruption in Kenya.

hechos/collateral-murder/titulo.texto: The 2007 Baghdad attack and the “Collateral Murder” video

hechos/collateral-murder/resumen.texto: In July 2007 two US helicopters killed about a dozen people in Baghdad, among them two Reuters journalists. WikiLeaks published the video of the attack on April 5, 2010, provided by Chelsea Manning, under the title “Collateral Murder”; the Pentagon maintained that the soldiers had followed the rules of engagement.

hechos/detencion-de-manning/resumen.texto: Manning was arrested on May 27, 2010 in Iraq, after the hacker Adrian Lamo, to whom she had described her leaks in a chat, reported her. She spent months in isolation at the Quantico base, in conditions the UN Special Rapporteur on Torture described as cruel and inhuman.

hechos/diarios-de-afganistan/resumen.texto: On July 25, 2010 WikiLeaks, The Guardian, The New York Times and Der Spiegel published some 75,000 military reports on the war in Afghanistan, with data on unreported civilian deaths. The Pentagon charged that they exposed Afghan informants.

hechos/registros-de-irak/resumen.texto: On October 22, 2010 WikiLeaks and several media outlets published some 390,000 military reports on the Iraq War, which recorded tens of thousands of civilian deaths and torture by Iraqi forces known to the US military.

hechos/cablegate/titulo.texto: Cablegate: the United States diplomatic cables

hechos/cablegate/resumen.texto: From 28 November 2010 WikiLeaks and five newspapers (among them El País) published, in edited form, cables from US embassies, a total of about 250,000. On 1 December Amazon removed WikiLeaks from its servers, after members of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, among them Joe Lieberman, asked about that hosting. In September 2011 all of them were released unedited, with the names of informants; the US government said this put lives at risk, and WikiLeaks blamed The Guardian.

hechos/operacion-payback/resumen.texto: Anonymous attacked, from September 2010, the sites of anti-piracy organizations and, in December, with denial-of-service attacks, the sites of PayPal, Visa, MasterCard and other companies that had cut off donations to WikiLeaks. The attempt to bring down Amazon’s site was abandoned for lack of participants. In 2013 several participants were convicted in the United States and the United Kingdom.

hechos/assange-contra-la-fiscalia-sueca/.texto: In 2010 Sweden requested Assange's extradition to question him over allegations of sexual offenses by two women, which he denied and attributed to a maneuver to hand him over to the United States. The UK Supreme Court approved the extradition on May 30, 2012. Sweden closed the investigation in 2019 without charging him.

hechos/asilo-de-assange/resumen.texto: On June 19, 2012 Assange sought asylum at the Embassy of Ecuador in London, which Rafael Correa's government granted in August. He lived there for almost seven years; a UN working group concluded in 2016 that he was arbitrarily detained, and the United Kingdom rejected that opinion.

hechos/detencion-de-assange/titulo.texto: Arrest of Assange and the United States extradition request

hechos/detencion-de-assange/resumen.texto: On April 11, 2019, when Ecuador withdrew his asylum, British police arrested Assange for having breached his bail. The United States charged him with conspiring with Manning to break into a military computer and with 17 counts under the Espionage Act, and requested his extradition; he spent more than five years in Belmarsh while the case was litigated.

hechos/acuerdo-de-assange/resumen.texto: On June 26, 2024, before a federal court in the Northern Mariana Islands, Assange pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to obtain and disclose national defense information. He was sentenced to time already served in Belmarsh and flew to Australia; his supporters celebrated his freedom and criticized the penalizing of a journalistic practice.

hechos/consejo-de-guerra-de-manning/resu.texto: After pretrial hearings starting in December 2011, a military court at Fort Meade acquitted her on July 30, 2013 of aiding the enemy, a charge that could carry life imprisonment, and convicted her on almost all the others, including violations of the Espionage Act. On August 21 it sentenced her to 35 years in prison.

hechos/conmutacion-de-manning/resumen.texto: On January 17, 2017, days before leaving office, Barack Obama commuted Chelsea Manning's sentence, and she left prison on May 17 after almost seven years in custody. Republican lawmakers criticized the decision as a signal of impunity for those who leak secrets.

hechos/revelaciones-de-snowden/resumen.texto: Starting on June 5, 2013 The Guardian, The Washington Post and other media published documents provided by Edward Snowden in Hong Kong on programs of the NSA and its allies: the collection of telephone metadata, PRISM, cable tapping and spying on allied governments. On June 9 Snowden revealed his identity.

hechos/snowden-en-rusia/resumen.texto: Charged by the United States and with his passport revoked, Snowden was stranded on June 23, 2013 in the transit zone of the Moscow airport, on his way to Latin America. On August 1 Russia granted him temporary asylum; in 2022 it granted him citizenship.

hechos/operacion-tunez/resumen.texto: In January 2011, during the revolution that toppled Ben Ali, Anonymous attacked websites of the Tunisian government, which censored the internet, and distributed tools to circumvent censorship. It repeated similar operations in Egypt and other countries of the Arab Spring.

hechos/ataque-a-hbgary/titulo.texto: The Anonymous attack on HBGary Federal

hechos/ataque-a-hbgary/resumen.texto: In February 2011, after the head of the security firm HBGary Federal said he had identified leaders of Anonymous, the group broke into its systems and published its emails. They revealed proposals to discredit journalists and WikiLeaks supporters.

hechos/lulzsec/resumen.texto: Anonymous splinter group that between May and June 2011 attacked Sony, the PBS network, the CIA website and US police forces, “for fun.” Its leader, Sabu, was already cooperating with the FBI, and in March 2012 its members were arrested in the United States, the United Kingdom and Ireland.

hechos/caso-jstor/titulo.texto: The JSTOR case against Aaron Swartz

hechos/caso-jstor/resumen.texto: Swartz downloaded millions of JSTOR articles by connecting a computer in a closet at MIT. Arrested in January 2011, he was charged by prosecutors with thirteen offenses carrying theoretical sentences of decades in prison; JSTOR did not pursue the case. He took his own life on January 11, 2013 and the charges were dropped; his family blamed the prosecutors and MIT.

hechos/fundacion-de-sci-hub/resumen.texto: Alexandra Elbakyan created in September 2011 a website that provides free access to paywalled scientific articles, obtained with university credentials. For publishers it is piracy and a security risk; for many researchers, a response to abusive prices.

hechos/juicios-contra-sci-hub/resumen.texto: Elsevier sued Sci-Hub in New York in 2015 and in 2017 obtained a default judgment of 15 million dollars; that same year the American Chemical Society won another of 4.8 million. Elbakyan did not appear, did not pay, and the site remained active under other domains.

hechos/apagon-contra-sopa-y-pipa/resumen.texto: On January 18, 2012 the English Wikipedia, Reddit and thousands of websites went dark or displayed protest notices against the SOPA and PIPA bills, and millions of people wrote to their legislators. Two days later both bills were postponed indefinitely.

hechos/bloque-genesis/resumen.texto: On January 3, 2009 Satoshi Nakamoto created the first block of the Bitcoin chain, with that day's headline from The Times about a new bank bailout. On January 12 Hal Finney received the first transaction.

hechos/silk-road/resumen.texto: Anonymous marketplace created by Ross Ulbricht in 2011 on the Tor network, where mainly drugs paid for with bitcoin were sold. The FBI shut it down in October 2013 and arrested Ulbricht in a San Francisco library.

hechos/condena-e-indulto-de-ulbricht/tit.texto: Conviction and pardon of Ross Ulbricht

hechos/condena-e-indulto-de-ulbricht/lug.texto: Daniel Patrick Moynihan Courthouse, New York

hechos/condena-e-indulto-de-ulbricht/res.texto: A New York jury found Ulbricht guilty in February 2015 and Judge Katherine Forrest sentenced him to life in prison without parole. His supporters considered the sentence disproportionate; on January 21, 2025 Donald Trump granted him a full pardon.

hechos/lanzamiento-de-ethereum/resumen.texto: The Ethereum network, proposed by Vitalik Buterin and funded in 2014 through a crowdsale of its currency, ether, went live on 30 July 2015, backed by a foundation based in Switzerland.

hechos/the-dao/titulo.texto: The DAO and the Ethereum split

hechos/the-dao/resumen.texto: The DAO, an investment fund run by smart contracts, raised some $150 million in ether; in June 2016 someone exploited a flaw to take a third of it. The community decided to change the chain's rules to return the funds, and those who opposed this continued with the original chain, Ethereum Classic.

hechos/usl-contra-bsdi/resumen.texto: AT&T's Unix subsidiary sued the company BSDi and the University of California in 1992 for distributing a version of BSD that allegedly contained Unix code. The 1994 settlement allowed BSD to be released after a few files were removed; the uncertainty of those years favored the spread of Linux.

hechos/sco-contra-ibm/resumen.texto: SCO sued IBM in 2003 for billions of dollars, claiming it had copied Unix code into Linux, and threatened Linux users. In 2010 a jury decided that the rights to Unix belonged to Novell and not to SCO, which went bankrupt; the case ended with a settlement in 2021.

hechos/oracle-contra-google/resumen.texto: Oracle sued Google for using Java's application programming interfaces in Android. On 5 April 2021 the Supreme Court ruled, six votes to two, that this use was legitimate (“fair use”), an outcome supported by the software industry and open-source advocates.

hechos/microsoft-compra-github/resumen.texto: Microsoft bought the largest open-source code hosting platform for $7.5 billion, a turnaround from its hostility at the start of the century; it had already joined the Linux Foundation in 2016. Some programmers moved their projects elsewhere out of distrust.

hechos/conectar-igualdad/resumen.texto: Program created by Decree 459 of 6 April 2010 that delivered millions of netbooks to students and teachers in public schools, dual-booting Windows and GNU/Linux. Its supporters present it as digital inclusion; its critics point to its costs and lack of pedagogical use. Mauricio Macri's government scaled it back and replaced it; it was relaunched in 2020 and has not been funded since 2024.

hechos/huayra-gnu-linux/resumen.texto: GNU/Linux distribution based on Debian and developed by the Argentine state for the Conectar Igualdad netbooks, which adopted it in 2013. It was released under the GPL license; it was later discontinued.

hechos/fundacion-de-reddit/titulo.texto: Founding of Reddit and the joining of Aaron Swartz

hechos/fundacion-de-reddit/resumen.texto: Steve Huffman and Alexis Ohanian, accepted into the first class of Y Combinator, launched Reddit in June 2005. Between November 2005 and January 2006 the site merged with Infogami, Aaron Swartz’s company, and Swartz became an equal partner in the new company, Not A Bug, and helped rewrite the software with web.py. He was given the title of co-founder; in 2011 Ohanian argued that the correct description was that Swartz’s company had been acquired by Reddit. Condé Nast bought Reddit in October 2006, and Swartz was asked to resign in January 2007.

hechos/open-library/resumen.texto: An Internet Archive project to create “a web page for every book published,” in which Aaron Swartz was the original engineer and led the technical team from 2006, together with Brewster Kahle and others. It uses the Infogami wiki software and publishes its code under the AGPL license. It offers digital copies of books on controlled digital lending. In June 2020 four publishers (Hachette, Penguin Random House, John Wiley & Sons and HarperCollins) sued the Internet Archive in a federal court in New York. On 25 March 2023 the court ruled against it for copyright infringement, and in 2024 the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit rejected the appeal. The Internet Archive maintains that lending one digital copy for each paper copy is legal, under the first-sale doctrine and fair use.

lugares/embajada-de-ecuador-en-londres/r.texto: Apartment in the Knightsbridge district where Julian Assange lived for almost seven years (2012–2019) as an asylee of Ecuador, unable to leave because the British police would have arrested him. In April 2019 Lenín Moreno's government withdrew his asylum and the police went in to take him.

lugares/prision-de-belmarsh/resumen.texto: Maximum-security prison in southeast London. Julian Assange was held there from his arrest in April 2019 until June 2024, while the United States' extradition request was being processed.

lugares/sede-de-la-nsa/resumen.texto: Headquarters, at Fort Meade (Maryland), of the United States National Security Agency, created in 1952 for signals intelligence and cryptography. Its mass surveillance programs were exposed in 2013 by the documents Edward Snowden handed over; Chelsea Manning was tried at the neighboring base.

lugares/gchq/resumen.texto: British signals intelligence agency, heir to the Bletchley Park codebreaking school, headquartered in Cheltenham. Snowden's documents revealed its Tempora program for intercepting submarine cables; in the 1970s three of its cryptographers had secretly arrived at public-key cryptography.

lugares/campus-de-microsoft/resumen.texto: Microsoft's headquarters in Redmond, near Seattle, since 1986. From there the company dominated the personal operating system market and waged its dispute with free software.

lugares/universidad-de-helsinki/resumen.texto: Finland's leading university. Linus Torvalds was studying computer science there when he wrote the Linux kernel in 1991, on a personal computer, and distributed it from a university server.

lugares/universidad-de-california-en-ber.texto: Public university where the Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD), the free variant of Unix, was developed from 1977 onward, and where Daniel Bernstein was studying when he sued the government over restrictions on the export of cryptography.

lugares/internet-archive/resumen.texto: Nonprofit digital library founded by Brewster Kahle in San Francisco, which keeps copies of the web (the Wayback Machine), books, films and software. In 2023 and 2024 the courts ruled in favor of the publishers that sued it for lending digitized books without permission.

lugares/pionen/resumen.texto: Data center of the company Bahnhof, installed in a former civil defense shelter dug into the rock beneath Stockholm. In 2010 it hosted WikiLeaks servers.

lugares/cuartel-disciplinario-de-fort-le.texto: Maximum-security military prison of the United States, in Kansas. Chelsea Manning was held there from 2011 and served her sentence until Barack Obama commuted it; she was released in May 2017.
